records.place: Guarilihue, near Coelemu, Itata Valley, Southern Chile

wine.name: Viejas Tinajas Cinsault
wine.grapes: Cinsault alone, from old, ungrafted, dry farmed bush vines.
wine.sites: A heritage vineyard at Guarilihue in the coastal hills of Itata, on granite with some quartz, dry farmed and open to the cool Pacific air; the house's 2018 sheet dates its planting to 1982.
wine.making: The grapes are destemmed by hand and the whole berries go into old clay tinajas, which the house calls centennial, where they ferment on their own yeasts in a gentle, semi carbonic manner. The wine is raised in the same tinajas, without any oak, and bottled with little intervention.
wine.glass: Pale, bright ruby; wild strawberry, red cherry and redcurrant over dried roses, a dusty, earthy note of the clay and a touch of white pepper; light bodied, with fine, dry tannin, fresh acidity and a savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Made for its freshness, it is lovely within three or four years of the vintage and holds well for a few more.
wine.serve: 13 to 14 degrees Celsius, a little cool; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: Old tinajas: the clay jars, many over a century old, in which the wine ferments and ages.
The denomination of the Itata, a subregion of Chile's Southern region under the wine zoning of 1994.
The dry inland country; some early vintages were labelled so, before the Itata name was used for Cinsault.

records.table: Viejas Tinajas Cinsault is De Martino's red from Guarilihue in Itata: old, dry farmed Cinsault fermented and aged in clay jars over a century old, with no oak at all. It is pale, dusty and full of wild strawberry, so pour it a little cool.
records.story: Pietro De Martino, an Italian immigrant, settled at Isla de Maipo, south of Santiago, and the house dates itself to 1934. The family has run it since, over four generations by its own account. For decades De Martino was a Maipo house of Cabernet Sauvignon and Carmenère, and it is credited with the first Chilean wine labelled as Carmenère, in 1996. Its turn came in 2010, when the family began buying the old clay tinajas that farmers in the south had used for centuries, and with the 2011 vintage it made a Cinsault from Itata in fourteen of them, the first Viejas Tinajas. The wine came from the dry hills of Guarilihue, where vines have grown since the Spanish settled Concepción in the sixteenth century. Its early vintages were labelled Secano Interior, because the Itata name could not then be used for such grapes; later ones carry Itata. Light, clay raised and low in alcohol, it stood against the ripe, oaked style of Chilean export reds. For a sommelier it is the bottle that put Itata Cinsault on export lists, and the plainest lesson in what clay does that oak does not.

others.name: Gallardía del Itata
others.note: The house's Itata range of Cinsault, País and Moscatel from the dry farmed hills.

others.name: Viejas Tinajas Muscat
others.note: A white Moscatel from Guarilihue, made and aged in the same old tinajas.

others.name: Alto de Piedras Carmenère
others.note: The single vineyard Carmenère of the house's home at Isla de Maipo.

traps: De Martino's winery is at Isla de Maipo in the Maipo; the Viejas Tinajas grapes come from Itata, far to the south.
Tinajas are clay jars, not oak barrels, and they give the wine no wood flavour.
Cinsault in Itata is old dry farmed bush vine country, not the País of the mission vines, though the two grow side by side.

report: The library's founding year 1934 stands; one critic's account has the founder buying the Isla de Maipo property in 1936 and a nephew arriving in 1947, both left out for want of a second source.

The vine age differs by vintage: the 2018 sheet dates the vineyard to 1982, other vintages speak of vines of thirty or thirty five years, so the record gives the 2018 sheet's year and says old vines elsewhere.

Recent vintages (2021 onwards) appear as Viejas Tinajas Tinto on the house's sheets and in reviews, with some whole bunches; the plan's name Viejas Tinajas Cinsault is the long standing label, but the integrator may wish to note the rename.
The 2014 vintage was a one off blend with Carignan from Maule, by the house's own page; the record teaches the Cinsault alone.

records.place: Guarilihue and Nipas, Itata Valley, Southern Chile

wine.name: Grand Itata Tinto
wine.grapes: Cinsault, by far the larger part, with a little País.
wine.sites: Old, dry farmed, head trained bush vines on the hills of Guarilihue in Itata, planted in 1960 by the importers' sheets, on granite and quartz with some clay, farmed with growers whose families have worked them for generations.
wine.making: Picked by hand, the whole berries ferment on their own yeasts in concrete, without temperature control, for about three weeks on the skins. The wine is then raised for about a year in concrete, with no oak, and bottled with little added.
wine.glass: Raspberry, sour cherry and pomegranate over dried herbs, rose petal and a stony, granite note; light to medium in body, with soft, fine tannin, bright acidity and a juicy, gently savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Made to drink young and fresh, within three or four years of the vintage, though a good year holds a little longer.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, a little cool; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The house's name for its Itata wines, a red Tinto and a white Blanco.
Spanish for red: here the Cinsault led red, as against the Blanco.
The denomination of the Itata, a subregion of Chile's Southern region.

records.table: Grand Itata Tinto is Rogue Vine's red from the dry granite hills of Guarilihue: mostly Cinsault with a little País, from bush vines planted in 1960, fermented and raised in concrete. It is light, juicy and fresh, so pour it a little cool.
records.story: Rogue Vine was begun in 2011 by two founders who had met teaching at the Universidad de Concepción, in a borrowed garage in the city, with grapes bought from the Itata hills to the north. The country they turned to is old wine land: vines were planted around Concepción within a generation of the Spanish settlement of 1550, and when Chile's wine law of 1994 drew its map, the Itata became a subregion of the Southern region. By the twenty first century its old Cinsault, País and Moscatel bush vines, dry farmed on granite, were mostly sold by the kilo to large wineries. The founders chose instead to work with small growers in Guarilihue and Nipas, on vineyards they describe as sixty years old and more, some far older, buying from the same families each year rather than owning the land. Their wines are picked early, fermented on native yeasts and raised without oak, at modest alcohol. The Grand Itata Tinto, from Cinsault planted in 1960, became the project's red, beside a Grand Itata Blanco of Moscatel and Riesling. For a sommelier it is the grower's Itata: the old granite hills in a light, fresh, honest glass.

others.name: Grand Itata Blanco
others.note: A white of Moscatel, Riesling and in some years Sémillon from the Colina Sur vineyard at Guarilihue, planted in 1922.

others.name: Super Itata Tinto
others.note: The house's other Itata red, a step beyond the Grand Itata in its range.

traps: Grand Itata Tinto is mostly Cinsault, not País, though a little País goes into the blend.
Rogue Vine buys from Itata growers rather than owning great estates; the vines are the growers', the making the founders'.
Grand is part of the label's name, not a classification or a rank under Chilean law.

cards.back: Cinsault, with a little País, from bush vines planted in 1960.

cards.front: In what vessel is Grand Itata Tinto fermented and raised?

records.place: Traiguén, Valle del Malleco, Southern Chile

wine.name: Sol de Sol Chardonnay
wine.sites: The house's original vineyard at Traiguén in the Malleco valley, some six hundred kilometres south of Santiago, planted in 1993 on clay of volcanic origin over granite, in a cool, wet climate that ripens slowly and keeps acidity high.
wine.making: The bunches are pressed whole and the juice fermented in French oak barrels, larger than the standard size and only a small share new. The wine then rests on its lees for about nine months with regular stirring, and only a small part goes through malolactic conversion, which keeps its edge.
wine.glass: Lemon, green apple and white peach over hazelnut, toast and a flinty, struck match note; taut and fresh, with lively acidity, a fine creamy texture from the lees and a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Good on release, it gains depth over five to eight years and a strong vintage keeps for a decade.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The name as the house prints it: sun of suns, the far southern label of Viña Aquitania.
The southern denomination around Traiguén, a protected name that may be followed by Traiguén.
The town in the Malleco where the vines grow, named on the label beside the valley.

records.table: Sol de Sol Chardonnay is Viña Aquitania's white from Traiguén in the Malleco, from vines planted in 1993 far south of Santiago: barrel fermented, rested on its lees and kept lean. It is taut, flinty and fresh, a cool climate Chardonnay to pour with fish.
records.story: Viña Aquitania began with two Bordeaux winemakers, the owner of Château Cos d'Estournel and the winemaker of Château Margaux, who in 1984 began searching Chile for a site of their own. In 1990, with a Chilean agronomist and winemaker of French descent as their partner, they bought land at the Quebrada de Macul, at the foot of the Andes in the Maipo, and the winery there was finished in 1993. That same year the Chilean partner persuaded his wife's family, farmers at Traiguén in the Malleco, some six hundred kilometres to the south, to plant Chardonnay on their land: by the house's account the first vineyard of the zone. The first wine, Sol de Sol Chardonnay, was made with the 2000 vintage. As the house tells it, the Malleco then had no denomination of its own, and the wine's success helped bring the valley into Chile's wine map. In 2002 a Champagne agronomist and old friend of the founders joined as a fourth partner, and a Sol de Sol sparkling wine followed. For a sommelier the Chardonnay is the wine that showed Chile's far south could ripen fine white grapes: cool, slow and tense.

others.name: Sol de Sol Brut Nature
others.note: A sparkling wine from the same Traiguén vineyards, with no dosage.

others.name: Aquitania Cabernet Sauvignon
others.note: The house's red from its home vineyard at the Quebrada de Macul in the Maipo.

traps: Viña Aquitania's winery is in the Maipo at the Quebrada de Macul, but Sol de Sol grows at Traiguén in the Malleco, far to the south.
The Malleco lies beyond the Bío Bío, the southern edge of the region record, not part of the Itata.
Sol de Sol is a brand of the house, not a vineyard name or a classification.

report: The planting year differs between sources: 1993 on the house's own pages and the importer's, 1991 on one critic's page and 1995 on a guide; the record keeps the house's 1993.
The two Bordeaux founders and the Champagne partner are described, not named: two of the three are living, and the dead one's dates were not found in two sources.
The house's claim that Sol de Sol helped create the Malleco denomination is told as the house's account; the year of the decree was not confirmed.
The Sol de Sol Pinot Noir named in the plan's note was not confirmed by any source read, so others carries the Brut Nature and the Maipo Cabernet instead.
The Malleco is a separate southern subregion beyond the Bío Bío; the region record counts it with Itata and Bío Bío, which the record follows.

records.place: Yumbel, Secano Interior, Bío Bío Valley, Southern Chile

wine.name: Pipeño
wine.grapes: País alone, the old mission grape of the Spanish settlers.
wine.sites: The family farm at Yumbel in the dry inland hills of the Bío Bío, its old, dry farmed País vines on trumao, the volcanic sand of redeposited ash, over an ancient lava flow.
wine.making: The grapes are picked by hand and ferment on their own yeasts in open vats of raulí, the native southern beech, with no pressing of the skins. The free run wine then rests on its fine lees for a few months in raulí casks, the pipas that give pipeño its name, and is bottled unfined, unfiltered and without added sulphur.
wine.glass: Pale and slightly cloudy; crushed red cherry, cranberry and wild strawberry over a rustic, earthy note of the old wood and a hint of dried herbs; light, juicy and fresh, with gentle, chalky tannin and a short, thirst quenching finish.
wine.ageing: A country wine for its first year or two, drunk young and fresh while its fruit is bright.
wine.serve: 12 to 14 degrees Celsius, cool from the cellar; no need to decant; a tumbler or a small red wine glass.

label.means: The traditional country wine of southern Chile, named for the pipa, the cask in which it rests.
The dry inland country of the south, unirrigated, where the old País vines grow.
The town of the family farm, in the Bío Bío, named on the label beside the appellation.

records.table: Cacique Maravilla's Pipeño is the old country wine of the Bío Bío: País from a family farm at Yumbel, fermented in open raulí vats and bottled in a litre with nothing added. It is light, juicy and rustic, so pour it cool.
records.story: The family behind Cacique Maravilla has farmed at Yumbel, in the dry inland hills of the Bío Bío, for seven generations, and by its own account its first País vines were planted in 1776, though another account puts the family's vines in the 1760s. The name, as the family tells it, was given to a forebear by the Mapuche of the district, who called him the Cacique Maravilla, the wondrous chief. For most of its history the farm made pipeño, the rough, fresh País of the southern countryside, fermented in open vats of raulí and sold in bulk or drunk at home. When Chile's wine law of 1994 drew its map, the Bío Bío became a subregion of the Southern region, but the old País and its pipeño stood outside the fine wine trade. The present generation turned that around: it bottled the farm's pipeño under the family's name, in a convivial litre bottle, and by the 2014 vintage the Pipeño País was reaching export lists and reviewers abroad. For a sommelier it is the pipeño as the south has always made it, with a bottle and a label: the plainest glass of the mission grape.

others.name: Vino Naranja
others.note: A skin contact white, left about two months on its skins in open raulí vats.

others.name: Naturalmente Tinto
others.note: A red of the farm, made in the same natural way as the Pipeño.

traps: Pipeño names a traditional style of light, rustic País, not a grape and not an appellation.
Raulí is the native southern beech, not oak; the vats and pipas of pipeño are traditionally made of it.
Yumbel is in the Bío Bío, not in the Itata, though both lie in Chile's Southern region.

report: No site of the house's own was found; every fact rests on two or more importers', retailers' or press pages, and the family's dates are told as its own account.

The region record's eighteenth century for the vines agrees: 1776 in two sources, the 1760s in one; the record gives 1776 as the family's account and names the other, and the founding year is left empty.
The forebear given the name, a Francisco Gutiérrez by one profile, arrived from the Canary Islands in 1750 by that one account only, so he is described, not named.
Some vintages are fermented in cement rather than raulí by one retail sheet; the record gives raulí, the house's usual account in three sources.
The label term Secano Interior and the town Yumbel are taken from two retail listings of the bottle; Decanter's 2014 review files it as Yumbel, Región Sur.
The living grower of the seventh generation is never named.

records.place: Nacimiento, Bío Bío Valley, Southern Chile

wine.name: Rivera del Notro
wine.grapes: País alone, from very old vines.
wine.sites: A single old vineyard outside Nacimiento, some eight hundred metres from the Bío Bío river, on alluvial soils; the vines are said to be two hundred years old and more.
wine.making: The grapes are picked by hand, destemmed by hand and gently crushed, then fermented on their own yeasts. The wine is raised for about a year, most of it in concrete and a small part in old barrels, and bottled with little intervention.
wine.glass: Red cherry, redcurrant and raspberry over eucalyptus, fresh mint and an iron, earthy note; light bodied and juicy, with firm, slightly rustic tannin, bright acidity and a fresh, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Open and juicy on release, it drinks well within four or five years, though its tannin carries a good vintage a little longer.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, a little cool; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The wine's name, given to both a red País and a white Itata blend.
Spanish for red: the País of the Bío Bío, as against the Blanco.
The Bío Bío Valley, a subregion of Chile's Southern region under the zoning of 1994.

records.table: Rivera del Notro is Roberto Henríquez's red from very old País vines outside Nacimiento, close to the Bío Bío river, hand destemmed and raised mostly in concrete. It is light and juicy, with cherry, mint and firm tannin, so pour it a little cool.
records.story: País came to Chile with the Spanish in the sixteenth century, and around Concepción and along the Bío Bío it was planted as the vine of the missions and the farms; some of those vineyards are said to be two centuries old. When Chile's wine law of 1994 drew its map, the Bío Bío became a subregion of the Southern region, yet its old País was seen as a grape of bulk wine. The grower behind this house was born in Concepción and trained as an agronomist at the university there, then made wine in Canada, South Africa and the Loire, where he learnt natural wine from a grower of Anjou, and worked beside a French natural winemaker in Chile. In 2015 he went out on his own, back in his home country of the Bío Bío, working old vineyards he rents rather than owns, in the Bío Bío and the Itata near the Nahuelbuta range, dry farmed and tended by organic and biodynamic methods without certification. Rivera del Notro, the red, comes from one of those old vineyards at Nacimiento. For a sommelier it is País taken seriously: the mission grape of the south made with care, light and fresh, yet with real grip.

others.name: Rivera del Notro Blanco
others.note: A white of the same name from Itata, of Moscatel, Corinto and Sémillon.

others.name: Santa Cruz de Coya
others.note: A País from vines said to be two hundred years old, in the Bío Bío.

others.name: Pipeño
others.note: The house's País pipeño, fermented in concrete and aged in old barrels.

traps: Rivera del Notro names both a red País from the Bío Bío and a white blend from Itata; the red is the one taught here.
País is the same grape as Mission in California and Criolla Chica in Argentina, not a local name for Cinsault.
The house works rented old vineyards; it is a grower's label, not an estate with vines of its own.

report: The house trades under the grower's own name; in prose the person is only the grower, and the Loire grower and the French winemaker in Chile he worked beside, both living, are described, not named.
No site of the house's own was found; the founding year 2015 rests on Afar, Raisin and the South America Wine Guide.

The ageing (about a year, mostly concrete, a fifth in old barrels) is from one retailer's note of the 2020 vintage, so the record says a small part in old barrels; a checker may cut it if no second source is found.
The vines' age of two hundred years and more is the importers' claim, told as said to be.
One listing gives the red as Cinsault; the producer's importers and other retailers give País, which the record follows.
The meaning of notro (a native shrub of southern Chile) was not sourced and is left out.
